_topic: Ethical Use of Artificial Intelligence in Academic Research

papers.title: Transparency and Accountability Frameworks for AI-Assisted Academic Research: A Systematic Review
papers.authors: Okonkwo, A. J., Ferreira, M. L., Nakamura, T.
papers.abstract: The proliferation of large language models in academic research workflows raises significant questions about authorship, attribution, and institutional accountability. This systematic review examined 87 policy frameworks and empirical studies published between 2020 and 2024. We identify three dominant paradigms: disclosure-only models, co-authorship models, and tool-use models. Our findings indicate that disclosure-only frameworks are insufficient without complementary verification mechanisms. We recommend that institutions adopt tiered governance frameworks calibrated to research risk level. Limitations include the rapid pace of change in AI capabilities and policy environments.

papers.title: Detecting AI-Generated Text in Student Submissions: A Comparative Evaluation of Detection Tools
papers.authors: Vasquez, C. R., Obi, N. K., Lindström, E.
papers.abstract: The widespread availability of generative AI writing assistants has created new challenges for academic integrity assessment. We evaluated seven commercially available AI-text detection systems across a corpus of 2,400 student submissions (1,200 fully human-written, 600 fully AI-generated, 600 hybrid). Detection accuracy ranged from 61% to 89% across tools, with false positive rates as high as 24% for non-native English speakers. These findings have significant implications for institutional reliance on automated detection as an integrity enforcement mechanism. We argue that detection-first approaches are insufficient and recommend a shift toward assessment design that reduces incentive for AI substitution.

papers.title: arXiv:2409.00001 — Towards Ethical AI Integration in Architectural Design Practice: Professional Responsibility and Disclosure Norms
papers.abstract: Generative AI tools are increasingly used in early-stage architectural design, raising questions about professional responsibility, copyright in AI-assisted design outputs, and client disclosure obligations. Through semi-structured interviews with 42 practicing architects across six countries, we explore current attitudes toward AI tool disclosure. Only 23% of respondents reported consistently disclosing AI tool use to clients. Regulatory frameworks were found to be absent in 80% of represented jurisdictions. We propose a preliminary disclosure framework aligned with existing professional codes of conduct and argue for professional body guidance updates.

papers.title: Bias Propagation in AI-Assisted Literature Reviews: Empirical Evidence from Biomedical Research
papers.authors: Singh, R. P., Eze, C. M., Hoffmann, J. L., Tanaka, Y.
papers.abstract: Automated literature review tools based on large language models may inherit and amplify existing biases in scholarly publication records. We conducted a controlled experiment in which 180 biomedical literature reviews were generated using three AI systems across six research topics with known demographic and geographic publication disparities. AI-assisted reviews systematically underrepresented research from low- and middle-income country institutions by 34% compared to manual reviews. Citation of studies with female lead authors was 18% lower in AI-generated reviews. These findings suggest that AI literature tools require explicit bias auditing mechanisms before deployment in systematic review contexts.

papers.title: Institutional Governance of AI Research Tools: Policy Survey Across 50 Universities
papers.authors: Nwosu, B. E., Chandra, V., Petrov, A. N.
papers.abstract: This survey examines AI governance policies across 50 research universities in 12 countries. Of the 50 institutions surveyed, 34 had issued AI policy guidance, 22 had mandatory disclosure requirements for AI-assisted research outputs, and only 8 had implemented technical governance controls. Policy content varied significantly: 64% addressed generative AI for writing assistance while only 28% addressed AI for literature review and data analysis. We identify four governance archetypes and discuss implementation challenges. The study concludes that current governance frameworks are largely reactive and that proactive, risk-calibrated approaches are needed.
